cards.q: Where does JavaScript run besides the browser?
cards.a: On servers and in tools through Node.js (and Deno or Bun), and in desktop apps built with Electron.
cards.lessonTitle: What JavaScript Is and Running It

cards.q: What does TypeScript add to JavaScript?
cards.a: Static types checked before the program runs; it compiles to plain JavaScript.
cards.lessonTitle: What JavaScript Is and Running It

cards.q: When should you use let instead of const?
cards.a: Only when the variable must be reassigned later.

cards.q: What does typeof null give?
cards.a: "object", a historical quirk; check for null with === null.

cards.q: Why prefer === to ==?
cards.a: === compares without converting types, so its result is predictable.

cards.q: What is the difference between a || b and a ?? b?
cards.a: || replaces any falsy a (including 0 and ""); ?? replaces only null and undefined.

cards.q: How do you insert a value into a string?
cards.a: With a template literal: `Total: ${total}`.

cards.q: Why is "😀".length 2?
cards.a: The emoji is stored as a surrogate pair of two UTF-16 code units.

cards.q: What is the difference between for...of and for...in?
cards.a: for...of gives the values of an iterable such as an array; for...in gives the keys of an object.

cards.q: What happens in a switch case without break or return?
cards.a: Execution falls through into the next case.

cards.q: What does an arrow function with braces return if it has no return statement?
cards.a: undefined.

cards.q: What is the difference between a rest parameter and spread?
cards.a: Rest collects arguments into an array in a definition; spread expands an array into separate arguments in a call.

cards.q: What does [10, 9, 1].sort() give, and why?
cards.a: [1, 10, 9]: without a compare function, items are compared as strings.

cards.q: Which methods change the array: map, splice, slice, sort?
cards.a: splice and sort; map and slice return new arrays.

cards.q: When must you use brackets instead of a dot to read a property?
cards.a: When the property name is in a variable or is not a valid identifier, such as "page count".

cards.q: Is { ...obj } a deep copy?
cards.a: No, a shallow one: nested objects are still shared; structuredClone makes a deep copy.

cards.q: What is a closure?
cards.a: A function together with the variables of the scope it was created in, which it keeps using later.

cards.q: Why does let fix the closure-in-a-loop problem?
cards.a: let creates a new binding for each iteration, so each callback remembers its own value.

cards.q: When is a Map better than a plain object?
cards.a: When keys are data that change at run time, or are not strings, and when you need size and reliable ordering.

cards.q: What does JSON.stringify do with a Map?
cards.a: Writes {} (its entries are lost); convert it with Object.fromEntries first.

cards.q: What does a # in front of a field name mean?
cards.a: The field is private: only code inside the class body can read or write it.

cards.q: Why must a subclass constructor call super() before using this?
cards.a: The parent's constructor creates and sets up the object; this does not exist until it has run.

cards.q: Where does a class's method live: on each instance or once on the prototype?
cards.a: Once on ClassName.prototype; every instance finds it through the prototype chain.

cards.q: Why does setTimeout(obj.method, 100) often break?
cards.a: The method is called later on its own, so this is undefined instead of obj; pass () => obj.method() or obj.method.bind(obj).

cards.q: Why throw new Error("...") instead of throw "..."?
cards.a: Error objects carry a name, a message and a stack trace, and can be checked with instanceof.

cards.q: What should a catch block do with an error it does not know how to handle?
cards.a: Rethrow it, so it is not silently hidden.

cards.q: What makes an object usable in for...of?
cards.a: A [Symbol.iterator]() method that returns an object with next() giving { value, done }.

cards.q: Why can a generator describe an infinite sequence?
cards.a: It is lazy: it only computes the next value when asked, so a consumer that stops early never runs forever.

cards.q: What is the difference between import { x } and import x?
cards.a: import { x } takes the named export x; import x takes the default export under any name you choose.

cards.q: If two files import the same module, does it run twice?
cards.a: No, it runs once; both get the same instance and share its state.

cards.q: Why does setTimeout(f, 0) not run f immediately?
cards.a: It puts f in the task queue; the event loop runs it only after the current code has finished and the microtasks have run.

cards.q: What happens to a page while a long synchronous loop runs?
cards.a: It freezes: no events, timers or redraws can run until the loop ends.

cards.q: What does then return?
cards.a: A new promise for the value returned by its callback (waiting for it if that is a promise).

cards.q: What is the difference between Promise.all and Promise.allSettled?
cards.a: all rejects as soon as one promise rejects; allSettled always waits for every promise and reports each outcome.

cards.q: What does an async function return if its body says return 5?
cards.a: A promise that fulfils with 5.

cards.q: Why is ids.forEach(async id => ...) a bug when you need to wait for the work?
cards.a: forEach ignores the promises the callback returns, so nothing waits for them and their errors are unhandled.

cards.q: Does fetch reject when the server answers 404?
cards.a: No: it fulfils with response.ok false; you must check ok or status yourself.

cards.q: How do you send a JavaScript object as a JSON body?
cards.a: method "POST", a Content-Type: application/json header, and body: JSON.stringify(object).

cards.q: What is the difference between debounce and throttle?
cards.a: Debounce runs once after the calls stop for a while; throttle runs at most once per period while calls keep coming.

cards.q: Why is next++ in the pool safe without locks?
cards.a: JavaScript runs one piece of code at a time; a worker can only be interrupted at an await, not in the middle of next++.

cards.q: Does TypeScript check types while the program runs?
cards.a: No: types are checked at compile time and removed; the running code is plain JavaScript.

cards.q: Why prefer unknown over any for data from JSON.parse?
cards.a: unknown forces you to check the value before using it; any switches checking off.

cards.q: An object has more properties than an interface asks for. Can it be passed where the interface is expected?
cards.a: Yes, as a variable: types are compared by shape. Only a fresh object literal with unknown properties is rejected.

cards.q: What is the difference between extends on an interface and & on types?
cards.a: Both combine members; extends builds a new interface from others, & makes an intersection type that has all members of both.

cards.q: What makes a union discriminated?
cards.a: Every variant has a shared property (like kind) with a different literal type, so checking it narrows to one variant.

cards.q: What does assigning to a variable of type never in the default case achieve?
cards.a: If any variant is not handled, the value is not never there and compiling fails, so new variants cannot be forgotten.

cards.q: What does K extends keyof T mean?
cards.a: K must be one of the property names of T.

cards.q: Why is first<T>(items: T[]): T better than first(items: any[]): any?
cards.a: It keeps the connection: calling it on numbers gives a number, so the result is still checked.

cards.q: What is the difference between private and # in a TypeScript class?
cards.a: private is checked only by the compiler; # fields are private at run time as well.

cards.q: What does Partial<Omit<Todo, "id">> describe?
cards.a: An object with any subset of Todo's fields except id, all optional.

cards.q: What does document.querySelector return when nothing matches?
cards.a: null.

cards.q: Why is el.innerHTML = userText dangerous?
cards.a: The text is parsed as HTML, so it can inject elements and scripts (XSS); textContent shows it as plain text.

cards.q: Why does one click listener on a ul work for list items added later?
cards.a: Click events bubble from the item up to the ul, so the listener on the ul sees them; that is event delegation.

cards.q: What type are the values from new FormData(form)?
cards.a: Strings (or File objects for file inputs); numbers must be converted.

cards.q: What does localStorage.getItem return for a key that was never set?
cards.a: null.

cards.q: Why wrap JSON.parse of stored data in try/catch?
cards.a: Stored data can be missing, corrupt or from an older version; reading it must not crash the app.

cards.q: Which versions does ^2.3.1 allow?
cards.a: From 2.3.1 up to, but not including, 3.0.0.

cards.q: Why commit package-lock.json?
cards.a: It records the exact version of every package, so every install gets the same code.

cards.q: Why keep update and render free of DOM and storage calls?
cards.a: They become pure functions that can be tested without a browser, and all side effects live in one small place.

cards.q: Why must render escape habit names?
cards.a: The HTML string is assigned to innerHTML, so unescaped user text could inject markup or scripts.

cards.q: What is the difference between `".+"` and `".+?"`?
cards.a: The first is greedy and runs to the last quote it can; the lazy one stops at the first closing quote.

cards.q: When do you need `new RegExp(...)` instead of `/.../`?
cards.a: When the pattern is built at run time, for example from user input or from pieces.

cards.q: Why does freezing an object not stop `settings.sizes.push(3)`?
cards.a: `Object.freeze` is shallow: the property `sizes` cannot be replaced, but the array it points to is not frozen.

cards.q: Why use a Symbol as a key instead of a string?
cards.a: A symbol is unique, so it cannot clash with any other property, and it stays out of `Object.keys` and JSON.

cards.q: Why call `Reflect.set(...)` inside a `set` trap instead of `obj[key] = value`?
cards.a: `Reflect.set` performs the normal assignment correctly (setters, the receiver) and returns whether it worked, which the trap must return.

cards.q: Why can a WeakMap not be iterated?
cards.a: Its entries vanish whenever the garbage collector removes their keys, so its contents are not something code could rely on.

cards.q: Why should money be stored in whole cents?
cards.a: Most decimal fractions cannot be stored exactly as doubles, so sums drift; integers below 2^53 are exact.

cards.q: What is `new Date(2026, 0, 31)`?
cards.a: 31 January 2026 in local time: months count from 0.

cards.q: What is `keyof { a: number; b: string }`?
cards.a: The union `"a" | "b"`.

cards.q: What does `satisfies` give you that a type annotation does not?
cards.a: The value is checked against the type, but keeps its own more precise type for later use.

cards.q: Why read a huge file as a stream instead of with `readFile`?
cards.a: A stream handles one piece at a time, so the program does not need memory for the whole file.

cards.q: What does `process.exit(2)` tell the program that started yours?
cards.a: That it failed: any non-zero exit code means failure, and the number can say which kind.
